name: Adam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at seven, paper from the corner shop, breakfast with my wife Nadia. Then I go to the lock-up behind the garage on Mill Lane, where I tinker with an old Land Rover I've had for twenty years. Afternoons I do the shopping with Nadia and we watch the quiz shows. I was a truck mechanic for forty years at a haulage depot, engines, brakes, gearboxes, until I stopped at sixty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the thing you're proudest of from your working years, and what do you do when something breaks now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I stopped because the depot closed and I didn't want to start again with strangers at my age. The work was dirty and steady and I was good at it. Nadia cleaned offices part-time. We pay the rent on a small terrace house, and with two small pensions there's nothing left over. I like things the way they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, a bit of hype, a bit of use. I wouldn't say much, honestly. At the pub the lads would say it's just another gadget, and I'd nod and have my pint. If it saves some office somewhere a few minutes, good luck to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing new. I don't use any of that stuff. I've got a phone that calls and texts. What I think about is whether prices keep going up. We pay 575 a month for the house and the energy bill is the worst, so I'd say my worry is how long the pension keeps pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep working on the Land Rover, because it keeps me busy and costs little. Nadia and I would carry on with our weekly shop at the discount supermarket. If the heating bill gets silly, I'd turn it down a degree and wear another jumper, I did that last winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels all right, honestly, steady. I'm not worried about machines. I'm a bit worried about my knee and my wife's hip, and what happens if we need help at home. That's what keeps me up some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate asking your daughter for help. When was the last time you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something big came up, like a car repair for Nadia's little Fiat or a broken boiler, we'd have to borrow from our daughter Samira. She'd say yes, but I'd hate asking. She's got two kids and a mortgage herself. So I'd put off the boiler and use electric heaters, which I know cost more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be stuck if banking moved to an app. What exactly would go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only part of this that touches me is the shops and the bank. If everything moves to an app, I'm stuck. I go into the branch on Fridays, and the girl behind the counter knows me. If that closes because a program is doing the job, I'd have to learn something I don't want to.

say: I wouldn't say much, I'd nod and have my **pint**.
I'd say it's just another **gadget** and good luck to the office that saves a few minutes.
think: I don't use any of it, so my real worry is whether the **pension** keeps pace with prices.
My **knee** and my wife's hip worry me more than machines.
do: Keep tinkering with the **Land Rover** because it's cheap and keeps me busy.
Carry on with the weekly shop at the **discount supermarket**.
Turn the **heating** down a degree and wear another jumper.
feel: It feels **steady**, with a quiet worry about health and help at home.
S0.quote: We'd have to borrow from our daughter Samira. She'd say yes, but I'd hate asking.
fieldNote: Contentment with **routine**, but one broken boiler away from asking his daughter.
Fear is practical: the branch, the app and the pension, not the technology.
Reserved, dry and slow to speak of feelings.

steps.text: Keep working on the Land Rover in the lock-up
Turn the heating down a degree and wear a jumper
Borrow from my daughter Samira only for a big repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I'd say at the pub that some of the office jobs will go, and good for us who never had one. But I'd say the banks and councils shouldn't cut the counters, because there are plenty of us who can't use a phone for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the world around us is going to move to screens faster. I think the pension office, the doctor's reception, the bank, they'd all want us to do it online. Nadia can manage a bit with the tablet our daughter gave her, but I can't be bothered. I'd be left standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Samira to teach Nadia to use the bank app, since she's more patient than me. I'd keep going to the branch for as long as it's open. I'd also write down all the numbers and passwords on a card, because I know what happens if I forget. And I'd get Nadia to book my doctor's appointments for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the world's moving a step ahead of me, and I'm too old to jump. It's not scary, just irritating. Like when they changed the trucks to computers at the depot and we all had to learn the diagnostic gear or get left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Nadia can manage the tablet and you can't be bothered. What would change that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would help is if banks and councils still kept a person on the phone. I wouldn't mind waiting. If they cut that, I'd be in trouble. I'd go in person, queue for an hour, and I'd be rude about it, which doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The depot cut five mechanics when the diagnostic computers came in. What did you see happen to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old depot got rid of five mechanics when the diagnostic computers came in, and they weren't the young ones. It's the people who can't move who get hurt. I'd be one of them, if I was still working. As it is, I'm retired and I'd be only half-hit.

say: I'd say the **banks and councils** shouldn't cut the counters, because many of us can't use a phone for everything.
I'd say good for us who never had an **office job**.
think: The pension office, the doctor and the bank will all push us **online**.
Nadia can manage a bit, but I'd be **left standing** there.
do: Ask Samira to teach Nadia the **bank app**.
Keep going to the **branch** while it's open.
Write passwords on a **card** and ask Nadia to book my doctor visits.
feel: It feels like the world is a step ahead and I'm too old to **jump**.
S1.quote: My old depot got rid of five mechanics when the diagnostic computers came in, and they weren't the young ones.
fieldNote: Fears the **online shift** of banks and clinics, not job loss.
Draws on the depot's computerisation as proof.
Lets his wife handle the learning, and admits he's stubborn.

steps.text: Ask Samira to teach Nadia the bank app
Keep queuing at the bank branch on Fridays
Write the passwords on a card and keep it in the wallet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick. Two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd say this at the pub and to anyone who'd listen: the government and the big firms can't spring this on us. Somebody's got to have a plan for the people who can't keep up, because there are millions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one that bothers me, because I'm sixty-four, I don't use any of it, and everything around me would change before I know what's happened. If the thinking side goes first, the money, the pension, the post office, all of it could change. And I've got no savings to ride it out. It's hard to say what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bank and ask for a plain answer about what happens to our money and the pension payments. I'd ask Samira to come every weekend and help us. I'd hold on to every pound, cut the Land Rover costs, no more repairs. And I'd keep a bit of cash in a tin, because I trust paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a road with a lorry coming and I can't move quickly. I'd be quiet at home and not tell Nadia how worried I am. I'd lie awake and think about every bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is the shortest warning. What would you do with the first week after hearing the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give me time to learn anything. If it was ten, I'd probably try, because I'd have no choice. At two years I'd be reacting, not preparing. The hands-on side comes later, so at least my old trade would last, but I'm not working anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell Samira not to send money. Why is that so hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Samira that if things go badly, she shouldn't bother sending money. She'd send it anyway, I know. That's the sort of person she is. I'd hate for her kids to lose out because of us, so I'd say it with a firm face and be sad about it at night.

say: I'd say **two years** isn't enough for anyone, and the government can't spring this on us.
I'd say somebody needs a **plan** for people who can't keep up.
think: Everything around me would change before I know what's **happened**.
With no **savings**, I couldn't ride out a bad year.
do: Ask the bank for a plain answer about our **money** and pension payments.
Ask Samira to come every **weekend** and help us.
Keep a bit of **cash** in a tin, because I trust paper.
feel: It feels like standing on a road with a **lorry** coming and I can't move quickly.
S2.quote: I'm sixty-four, I don't use any of it, and everything around me would change before I know what's happened.
fieldNote: The **shortest warning** leaves him with reaction only.
Hides his fear from his wife, shows protective instincts.
Trusts paper and cash, which is how his resistance appears as a coping method.

steps.text: Ask the bank in person how our pension payments are protected
Ask Samira to visit every weekend and help with forms
Stop spending on Land Rover repairs
Keep a cash tin at home and watch the news

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to take in, but five years gives people a fighting chance. I'd say the government should start now with plain-speaking help for older folk, because they'll be the ones who get lost. I'd say it quietly, I'm not a speech-maker, but I'd sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-nine, so I'd still have a decade or more ahead. That's long enough for changes to hit us, but not so fast that I can't plan. I'm still wary. If the banks and the post office went fully online, we'd need Samira all the time, and she's got her own life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by making sure Nadia knows how to do the banking, the shopping online, all that. I'd learn the minimum myself, maybe the phone's camera and a video call to see the grandkids. I'd save 20 a month in the post office, and I'd clear out the garage, sell the spare Land Rover parts and keep that money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow wave you can see far off. I'm less tense than with two years. It gives me a bit of room to think and be stubborn without being stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be able to do by the end of the five years that you can't do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me do what I'd never do otherwise. I might even try the assistant thing if Nadia sits next to me. But the truth is, if I'm left alone with it, I'd stop. I need someone patient, not one of those videos where a kid talks fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the spare Land Rover parts. How much do you think that would bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were a course for older people at the community centre, taught by someone my age, I'd go. I'd bring a flask and a biscuit. I'd want to learn on a machine that's not mine, so I can't break it. That's how I learned the diagnostic gear at the depot.

say: I'd say five years gives people a **fighting chance** if the government starts with plain help for older folk.
I'd **sign a petition**, though I'm not a speech-maker.
think: I'd be sixty-nine with a decade ahead, **wary** but able to plan.
If banking went fully online, we'd need **Samira** all the time.
do: Make sure **Nadia** can do the banking and online shopping.
Learn the minimum myself: the phone **camera** and a video call with the grandkids.
Save **20 a month** and sell spare Land Rover parts.
feel: It feels like a **slow wave** far off, and I'm less tense.
S3.quote: If there were a course for older people at the community centre, taught by someone my age, I'd go. I'd bring a flask and a biscuit.
fieldNote: More time lets him accept **minimal learning**, if patient and on someone else's machine.
Learned the depot's diagnostic gear that way once.

steps.text: Join a community centre course for older people on phones
Save 20 a month at the post office
Have Nadia learn banking and online shopping first
Sell spare Land Rover parts to add to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's a long way off, and a lot of what's said today will be forgotten by then. I'd say let's get on with the practical things and not panic. If someone asks, I'd say the older folk will need help, and the government should have a plan, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be seventy-four. A lot can happen to our health in ten years, honestly more than any computer would do. I'd think the machines will matter more to Samira's kids than to us. But I'd still want to know the pension is safe, and I'd rely on Nadia to read the small print.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the garage and the shopping. I'd save 15 a month, and I'd keep helping Samira's boy with his bike and his school project. I'd gradually learn the basics, maybe with the community course. And I'd keep paper copies of everything, the letters and statements, in a folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels far away, a bit like the end of the world on the telly, interesting but not in your kitchen. I'm calmer than in the short ones. I'd still be wary of banks and bureaucrats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is the longest warning. What does that change about how you would handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd get used to it slowly, the way I got used to mobile phones. I didn't like them either. I'd say it's best to wait until the thing's proven, then learn it on my terms. The worst bit is rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your grandson about your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandson that a trade is a good thing to have. A machine might fix a car one day, but someone has to tell it which noise is wrong. I'd say learn the machine, and learn to use your hands, both. I'd tell him that over a cup of tea.

say: I'd say let's get on with **practical things** and not panic.
I'd say the government should have a **plan** in writing for older folk.
think: A lot can happen to our **health** in ten years, more than any computer would do.
The machines will matter more to **Samira's kids** than to us.
do: Carry on with the garage, shopping and **paper copies** of every letter.
Save **15 a month** and keep helping my grandson with his bike.
Learn the **basics** slowly with a community course.
feel: It feels **far away**, like the end of the world on telly, not in my kitchen.
S4.quote: A machine might fix a car one day, but someone has to tell it which noise is wrong.
fieldNote: Ten years allows him to see the change as **slow** and manageable.
Passes on trade pride to his grandson.
Still wary of banks and bureaucrats, but calmer.

steps.text: Keep tinkering in the lock-up and keep paper copies of letters
Save 15 a month in the post office
Help my grandson with his bike and school project
Learn the basics on a community course over several years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to get used to it, and I'd have no money behind me. What would help is a person on the phone at the bank and the pension office, a proper plan from the government in plain words, and someone patient to teach us. Also, no more branch closures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that older people aren't daft, we're cautious. When I was a mechanic, I never trusted a part until I'd seen it work. Show me who's responsible if it breaks, and then I'll think about it.

headlineQuote: I never trusted a part until I'd seen it work. Show me who's responsible if it breaks, and then I'll think about it.
portrait: Adam is **64**, a retired truck mechanic living with his wife Nadia on two small pensions.
He doesn't use AI and is wary of **banks and offices** moving online.
He is dry, practical, and most afraid of **prices**, health and needing his daughter's help.
His mood is **uneasy** in quiet worlds and **alarmed** if change comes in two years.
biggestWorry: Two years worries him most, since there'd be **no time** to get used to it and no money behind him.
whatWouldHelp: A **person on the phone** at the bank and pension office, a plain government plan and patient teaching.
